column11: Menachot 110a: ‘Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya raised an objection to the statement of Rav from the verse: “From the rising of the sun until it sets, My name is great among the nations; and in every place offerings are presented to My name, and a pure meal offering; for My name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 1:11). column11: Berakhot 5a: ‘With regard to the verse: “For I have given you a good portion,” Rabbi Zeira, and some say Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa, said: Come and see how the characteristics of the Holy One, Blessed be He, are unlike the characteristics of flesh and blood. It is characteristic of flesh and blood that when one sells an object to another person, the seller grieves the loss of his possession and the buyer rejoices. With regard to the Holy One, Blessed be He, however, this is not so. He gave the Torah to Israel and rejoiced, as it is stated: “For I have given you a good portion, My Torah, do not abandon it.” A good portion is understood as a good purchase; although God sold Torah to Israel, He rejoices in…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 5a) to illuminate his exposition here (“meriting the three gifts granted through suffering: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come (ibid.). column11: Bava Metzia 87a: ‘Until Jacob, there was no illness leading up to death; rather, one would die suddenly. Jacob came and prayed for mercy, and illness was brought to the world, allowing one to prepare for his death, as it is stated: “And one said to Joseph: Behold, your father is sick” (Genesis 48:1), which is the first time that sickness preceding death is mentioned in the Bible. Until Elisha, one did not fall ill and then heal, as everyone who fell ill would die. Elisha came and prayed for mercy and he was healed, as it is written: “Now Elisha fell ill with his illness from which he was to die” (II Kings 13:14). By inference, one can derive that he had previously fallen ill with other illnesses from…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Metzia 87a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And until Elisha no sick person ever recovered from mortal illness (Bava Metzia 87a), because the revelation of healing for the wound of circumcision had not yet appeared in deed, for which the angel Raphael...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: That a handful of dust covers the covetous eye which is never satisfied with any pleasure, and outweighs all gold, see there. Therefore, this burial place of the Patriarchs who encompass the entire world, is “at the end of the field” of Ephron, who was the evil-eyed one as our Sages noted (Bava Metzia 87a) (and so it is in gematria: “ra ayin” = 400), he being evil-eyed and never satisfied with little; and this exists for him at the end of his field, and when a person eventually dies they show him burial which points to this truth.

column15: Just as it is related in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 84a): Originally, when Rabbi Yochanan stated a teaching, Reish Lakish would raise twenty-four objections against him, [and Rabbi Yochanan would provide twenty-four resolutions,] and consequently the teaching became vastly clarified and broadened. This illustrates that Hashem determined that all genuine breakthroughs and assistance must emerge specifically through an opposing force; and this is the Rabbinic maxim: “If he merits, it is a helper (ezer); if he does not merit, it is against him (kenegdo).”

column11: Yoma 39a: ‘Conversely, the Sages taught the following with regard to the verse: “Sanctify yourselves and you will be sanctified” (Leviticus 11:44); a person who sanctifies himself a bit, they sanctify him and assist him greatly. If a person sanctifies himself below, they sanctify him above. If a person sanctifies himself in this world, they sanctify him in the World-to-Come.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 39a) to illuminate his exposition here (“sanctifying himself a little below in this world, whereby they sanctify him abundantly from Above in the World to Come (Yoma 39a), meriting the healing of the wound: consummate holiness requiring no further...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And another Sage answered: "she spread a sheet of white linen, and never saw a nocturnal emission upon it"; even though the weariness of travel induces seminal emission sometimes even in the pious (Shabbat 127b). And from such involuntary bodily occurrences man cannot protect himself through mortal striving alone; but only through being guarded from Above in proportion to how one sanctifies himself below (Yoma 39a); and whoever consecrates himself below to the utmost limit of human capacity, Heaven sanctifies him with boundless divine energy.

column13: And this is what they taught in Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah (chapter 5): that he merited a life devoid of sorrow and devoid of the evil inclination, and this is a foretaste of the World to Come. And just as Israel likewise merited this at the time of the Giving of the Torah, after the Holy One, blessed be He, brought down the dew of resurrection to revive them, and they merited that sublime vitality that will prevail after the resurrection of the dead, which is freedom from the evil inclination and from subjugation to the exiles.

column15: And this is why he strikes him on the mouth, as it is taught (Shabbat 33b): “The mouth concludes and completes.” For through this strike whereby the light was forgotten, his spiritual form as an agent of free choice was completed, empowered to acquire the light through his own initiative now that the primordial light was concealed from him; and though his evil inclination entices him to act contrary to the divine Will, man through his righteous choice overcomes it to serve his Creator, earning the light on his own merit so that it is called “the toil of his own hands”—which is man's ultimate purpose.
